html:
The Yup'ik and Cup'ik are Indigenous peoples of southwestern Alaska, around the deltas of the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers and the shores of the Bering Sea. Cup'ik is the name used by speakers of a dialect around Chevak and on Nunivak Island. They speak Central Alaskan Yup'ik, the most widely spoken Native language in Alaska.

They are related to the Inuit and Iñupiat to the north and share ancestry with the Thule people and older Bering Sea cultures. Their land is wet tundra laced with rivers and lakes. They lived by salmon fishing, hunting seals and walrus from kayaks, and hunting caribou and birds. Winter villages centred on a men's house, the qasgiq, where ceremonies were held with carved masks.

Russian traders and Orthodox missionaries reached the region in the early 1800s, during Russian America. After the Alaska Purchase of 1867, Moravian and Catholic missions followed. Epidemics hit hard, among them the great sickness of 1900 and the influenza of 1918. Many Yup'ik still live largely by fishing and hunting.
